THE OUTSIDE SALESPERSON EXEMPTION (LAB. CODE § 1171; WAGE ORDER 4-2001, §§ 1(C), 2(M); WAGE ORDER 7-2001, §§ 1(C), 2(J); RAMIREZ V. YOSEMITE WATER CO.) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Acme, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe what California law says about the outside salesperson exemption from the state’s wage and hour requirements — the exemption that is in question for a position such as Territory Sales Representative, held by Jordan Lee. It describes the statutory exclusion in Labor Code section 1171; the Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders’ definition of “outside salesperson” and the provision stating that the orders do not apply to such employees; the absence of any salary condition in that provision; the California Supreme Court’s holding in Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. that California uses a quantitative more-than-half-the-working-time test rather than the federal “primary function” test; how working time is counted, including travel time and delivery work; the “realistic requirements of the job” rule; the narrow construction of overtime exemptions and the employer’s burden of proof; and the limits of what the exclusion reaches. It describes the law; it does not classify any employee as exempt or nonexempt and does not evaluate any particular job.

THE STATUTORY EXCLUSION IN LABOR CODE SECTION 1171
California’s wage, hour, and working-conditions statutes for employees are gathered in Chapter 1 of Part 4 of Division 2 of the Labor Code, sections 1171 through 1207. The first section of that chapter, section 1171, states the chapter’s coverage: it applies to men, women, and minors employed in any occupation, trade, or industry, whether compensation is measured by time, piece, or otherwise, but it does not include any individual employed as an outside salesman, or any individual participating in a national service program carried out with assistance under section 12571 of title 42 of the United States Code.

Section 1171 does not itself define “outside salesman.” The definition used in California comes from the Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders, which are described in the next clause. In Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co., the California Supreme Court framed the question before it as whether an employee who performs a mixture of sales and nonsales duties is an “outside salesperson” within the meaning of section 1171, and described the answer as turning on a detailed, fact-specific determination of how the employee spent his time.

THE WAGE ORDERS’ QUANTITATIVE DEFINITION OF “OUTSIDE SALESPERSON”
Each Industrial Welfare Commission wage order defines “outside salesperson” in its definitions section, and the definition is the same across the orders that were checked for this document. It has four elements: the person is 18 years of age or over; the person customarily and regularly works more than half the working time away from the employer’s place of business; the work done away from the employer’s place of business is selling tangible or intangible items, or obtaining orders or contracts for products, services, or use of facilities; and both conditions — the location and the more-than-half measure — are stated in terms of how the working time is actually spent.

The definition appears at section 2(M) of Wage Order 4-2001, which covers professional, technical, clerical, mechanical, and similar occupations, and at section 2(J) of Wage Order 7-2001, which covers the mercantile industry. The wording in the two orders is identical.

THE WAGE ORDER DOES NOT APPLY AT ALL TO AN OUTSIDE SALESPERSON
A wage order states at its Section 1 that it applies to all persons employed in the covered occupations or industry, whether paid on a time, piece rate, commission, or other basis, subject to the exceptions that follow. One of those exceptions, section 1(C), states that the provisions of the order do not apply to outside salespersons.

That exception is written without any carve-out. It can be compared with the exception immediately before it: section 1(B), which excludes employees directly employed by the State or a political subdivision, preserves the application of Sections 1, 2, 4, 10, and 20 of the order to those employees. Section 1(C) contains no such list. By its terms, therefore, no provision of the order — including the sections on hours and days of work, minimum wages, reporting time pay, records, meal periods, rest periods, and uniforms and equipment — applies to a person who meets the order’s definition of outside salesperson. The same section 1(C) language appears in Wage Order 7-2001.

NO MINIMUM SALARY OR EARNINGS CONDITION APPEARS IN THE OUTSIDE SALESPERSON PROVISION
The executive, administrative, and professional exemptions in section 1(A) of the wage orders each carry an earnings condition in addition to a duties test: the employee must earn a monthly salary equivalent to no less than two times the state minimum wage for full-time employment, with full-time employment defined by Labor Code section 515(c) as 40 hours per week.

Section 1(C), the outside salesperson provision, states no earnings condition, no salary-basis condition, and no minimum-compensation figure. The only conditions that appear anywhere in the wage order for outside salesperson status are the ones in the definition at section 2(M) of Wage Order 4-2001 and section 2(J) of Wage Order 7-2001: age, location of the work, the nature of the work, and the more-than-half-the-working-time measure.

CALIFORNIA’S QUANTITATIVE TEST COMPARED WITH THE FEDERAL “PRIMARY FUNCTION” TEST
In Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co., the California Supreme Court held that the state’s outside salesperson definition is not to be read through the federal regulations. The federal exemption in effect at that time asked what the employee’s chief duty or primary function was, and then treated all work incidental to and in conjunction with the employee’s own sales — including incidental deliveries and collections — as exempt work. The court described the federal test as focused on defining the employee’s “primary function,” not on how much work time is spent selling.

The California wage order, the court explained, contains no provision that reclassifies intrinsically nonexempt nonsales work as exempt on the ground that it is incidental to sales. The court concluded that by adopting a distinct definition rather than tracking the federal language, the Industrial Welfare Commission intended to depart from federal law and to provide, at least in some cases, greater protection for employees. A court or a trier of fact applying the California definition therefore measures the share of working time spent on the activities the definition names, rather than characterizing the job as a whole.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Thus, the federal exemption focuses on defining the employee’s “primary function,” not on how much work time is spent selling."
  — Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785 (CourtListener text), 20 Cal.4th 785, 797 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1133701/ramirez-v-yosemite-water-company/)
  "State law also differs from the federal regulation in that it does not contain any provision that reclassifies intrinsically nonexempt nonsales work as exempt based on the fact that it is incidental to sales."
  — Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785 (CourtListener text), 20 Cal.4th 785, 797 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1133701/ramirez-v-yosemite-water-company/)
  "By choosing not to track the language of the federal exemption and instead adopting its own distinct definition of “outside salespersons,” the IWC evidently intended to depart from federal law and to provide, at least in some cases, greater protection for employees."
  — Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785 (CourtListener text), 20 Cal.4th 785, 797 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1133701/ramirez-v-yosemite-water-company/)

The federal regulations the court compared (29 C.F.R. former §§ 541.5, 541.505) were replaced by the Department of Labor in 2004; the current federal outside sales regulations were not fetched for this document, and this clause does not describe them. The Ramirez opinion was verified by two independent fetches of the CourtListener opinion page using different browser header sets, and each quoted phrase was separately confirmed through CourtListener’s public search index; no second publisher’s text of the opinion was reachable from this environment.

HOW WORKING TIME IS COUNTED: ACTUAL TIME FIRST, MEASURED AGAINST THE REALISTIC REQUIREMENTS OF THE JOB
Because the California test is quantitative, Ramirez addressed how the hours are to be counted: by the employer’s job description and estimate of what the employee should be doing, or by the hours the employee actually spent. The court held that neither alternative alone is satisfactory. Counting by the job description would let an employer make an employee exempt simply by writing an idealized description with little basis in reality; counting only actual hours would let an employee who falls below the 50 percent mark through his or her own substandard performance escape an otherwise valid exemption.

The court resolved the problem by directing the trier of fact to inquire into the realistic requirements of the job: to consider, first and foremost, how the employee actually spends his or her time, and also whether the employee’s practice diverges from the employer’s realistic expectations, whether there was any concrete expression of employer displeasure over substandard performance, and whether those expressions were themselves realistic given the actual overall requirements of the job.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "On the one hand, if hours worked on sales were determined through an employer’s job description, then the employer could make an employee exempt from overtime laws solely by fashioning an idealized job description that had little basis in reality. On the other hand, an employee who is supposed to be engaged in sales activities during most of his working hours and falls below the 50 percent mark due to his own substandard performance should not thereby be able to evade a valid exemption."
  — Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785 (CourtListener text), 20 Cal.4th 785, 802 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1133701/ramirez-v-yosemite-water-company/)
  "A trial court, in determining whether the employee is an outside salesperson, must steer clear of these two pitfalls by inquiring into the realistic requirements of the job. In so doing, the court should consider, first and foremost, how the employee actually spends his or her time. But the trial court should also consider whether the employee’s practice diverges from the employer’s realistic expectations, whether there was any concrete expression of employer displeasure over an employee’s substandard performance, and whether these expressions were themselves realistic given the actual overall requirements of the job."
  — Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785 (CourtListener text), 20 Cal.4th 785, 802 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1133701/ramirez-v-yosemite-water-company/)
  Known gap: In the CourtListener text of Ramirez the italicized words “should” and “realistic” appear on their own lines inside this passage; the line breaks were closed up so that the quoted sentences read continuously, which is a benign line-wrap artifact of the source’s formatting and changes no words. The same “realistic requirements of the job” language was later written into section 1(A) of the wage orders for the executive, administrative, and professional exemptions, which are separate exemptions addressed by other documents in this corpus and not by this one. How any particular employee’s time was in fact spent is a question of fact that this document does not address.

TRAVEL TIME AND THE APPORTIONMENT OF MIXED TRIPS
The employer in Ramirez argued that a strict reading of the wage order would produce an absurd result, because even full-time salespeople spend much of the day on preparation, travel, and paperwork rather than on face-to-face selling. The California Supreme Court answered that the order need not be read that strictly. Travel undertaken in order to attempt a sale counts as time spent selling: the court gave the example of a salesperson who must travel one hour to a destination to attempt a sale, and said the most reasonable interpretation of the wage order is to count that hour of travel as time spent selling.

Where a single trip serves both purposes, the court held that the travel time must be apportioned between the two types of activity for purposes of determining the total amount of time spent doing sales and nonsales work.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "If a salesperson must travel one hour to destination A in order to attempt a sale, then surely the most reasonable interpretation of the wage order is to count the hour of travel time as time spent “selling.” But if, as in the present case, an employee travels to a destination to engage in both sales and nonsales activities, the travel time must be apportioned among the two types of activities for purposes of determining the total amount of time spent doing sales and nonsales work."
  — Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785 (CourtListener text), 20 Cal.4th 785, 801 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1133701/ramirez-v-yosemite-water-company/)
  Known gap: The court did not state a formula or method for apportioning travel time on a mixed trip, and no source cited in this document supplies one. Whether travel time is compensable hours worked for an employee who is not an outside salesperson is a different question governed by other authority (including Morillion v. Royal Packing Co. and the wage orders’ “hours worked” definition) that this clause does not address; the passage quoted here goes only to whether travel counts toward the more-than-half measure in the outside salesperson definition. The characterization of the employer’s argument in the body summarizes the opinion’s description of that argument.

DELIVERY AND SERVICE WORK IS NOT COUNTED AS SELLING
Ramirez involved a route sales representative who delivered bottled water and was also expected to sign up new customers. The California Supreme Court stated that delivering preordered water bottles or restocking empties is not a sales activity in the conventional meaning of the word, and that a person who only performed those delivery tasks could not be considered a salesperson. The court rejected the argument that delivery becomes a sales activity because poor delivery would cost the customer, comparing that reasoning to treating an attorney’s preparation of a brief as a sales activity because it keeps the client.

Because the trial court and the Court of Appeal had applied the federal standard, or a hybrid of the federal and state standards, the Supreme Court reversed and remanded rather than deciding the employee’s status itself.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Delivery of preordered water bottles or the restocking of “empties” is not a sales activity in the conventional meaning of the word—one who only performed these delivery tasks could not be considered a salesperson. It is true, as Yosemite points out, that failure to properly deliver the product would lead to loss of the customer, but that does not make such delivery a sales activity, any more than an attorney’s preparation of a legal brief in order to satisfy and thereby retain a client is a sales activity."
  — Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785 (CourtListener text), 20 Cal.4th 785, 802 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1133701/ramirez-v-yosemite-water-company/)
  Known gap: The passage quoted below is the court’s characterization of the particular tasks in that case; it is not a general list of activities that do or do not count as selling, and the court did not decide whether the plaintiff was an outside salesperson, remanding instead for the trial court to resolve conflicting evidence about how his time was spent. The statement in the body that the case was reversed and remanded reflects the opinion’s disposition as stated in the fetched text; no separate quotation of the disposition is included below.

NARROW CONSTRUCTION OF THE EXEMPTION AND THE EMPLOYER’S BURDEN OF PROOF
Ramirez set out two general principles before construing the exemption. First, because the statutes regulating wages, hours, and working conditions are remedial and are liberally construed to promote the protection of employees, exemptions from the state’s mandatory overtime provisions are narrowly construed. Second, the assertion of an exemption from the overtime laws is an affirmative defense, so the employer bears the burden of proving the employee’s exemption.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Thus, under California law, exemptions from statutory mandatory overtime provisions are narrowly construed."
  — Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785 (CourtListener text), 20 Cal.4th 785, 794 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1133701/ramirez-v-yosemite-water-company/)
  "Moreover, the assertion of an exemption from the overtime laws is considered to be an affirmative defense, and therefore the employer bears the burden of proving the employee’s exemption."
  — Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785 (CourtListener text; star-pagination marker removed), 20 Cal.4th 785, 794-795 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1133701/ramirez-v-yosemite-water-company/)
  Known gap: The second quotation below spans a page break in the official reporter: in the CourtListener text the star-pagination marker “*795” appears between “proving the” and “employee’s exemption,” and that marker was removed from the quote as a benign reporting artifact; the quote is otherwise verbatim. Both statements are framed by the court as general rules about overtime exemptions rather than rules peculiar to the outside salesperson exemption, and the same two passages are relied on elsewhere in this corpus for other exemptions. Neither statement addresses the standard of proof or how the burden operates procedurally in any particular proceeding.

THE VALIDITY OF THE INDUSTRIAL WELFARE COMMISSION’S DEFINITION
The employer in Ramirez argued that the Industrial Welfare Commission had exceeded its authority by adopting a definition of “outside salesperson” narrower than the federal one, since the Legislature had borrowed a term already defined in federal law. The California Supreme Court rejected the argument. It held that the definition was within the scope of the Commission’s authority and was reasonably necessary to effectuate the purpose of section 1171: some working definition was needed because employees often work in both sales and nonsales capacities, and it was reasonable for the Commission to take a quantitative approach, looking to the actual hours spent on sales activity. The court added that the definition would be entitled to deference in any event, having been adopted through public notice and comment and consistently maintained for nearly 20 years.

The Legislature has separately referred to the outside salesperson category in Labor Code section 517, subdivision (d), which directed the Commission to conduct a review of the wages, hours, and working conditions of outside salespersons notwithstanding section 1171 and section 515, subdivision (a).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "It was necessary for the IWC to establish some working definition of “outside salesperson” that takes into account the fact that some employees work in both sales and nonsales capacities. It was reasonable for the IWC, in formulating its definition, to take a quantitative approach, looking to the actual hours spent on sales activity to determine if an employee is primarily a salesperson."
  — Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785 (CourtListener text), 20 Cal.4th 785, 801 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1133701/ramirez-v-yosemite-water-company/)
  "Notwithstanding sections 1171 and subdivision (a) of Section 515, the Industrial Welfare Commission shall conduct a review of wages, hours, and working conditions of outside salespersons."
  — California Labor Code § 517(d) (Official California Legislative Information), Lab. Code § 517, subd. (d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=517.)
  Known gap: The review that section 517, subdivision (d), directed was to be concluded by a deadline that has long passed, and that subdivision is quoted here only to show that the Legislature addressed the category; it does not state the substance of any regulation the Commission adopted, and this document does not describe the results of that review. The statements in the body about notice-and-comment adoption and long-standing maintenance summarize the opinion’s deference discussion; only the passage on the Commission’s authority and the quantitative approach is quoted below. The wage order the court upheld was Wage Order No. 7-80; the operative orders today are the 2001 orders quoted elsewhere in this document, which carry forward the same definitional language.

WHAT THE OUTSIDE SALESPERSON EXCLUSION DOES NOT REACH
The exclusion described in this document is bounded in several ways that appear on the face of the authorities. Labor Code section 1171 excludes an outside salesman from “this chapter” only — Chapter 1 of Part 4 of Division 2 of the Labor Code. It says nothing about Labor Code provisions located in other chapters, parts, or divisions, and nothing about federal law, local ordinances, or contract terms. Wage order section 1(C) makes the provisions of that order inapplicable, and each order covers only the industries or occupations its Section 1 describes.

The definition itself sets limits as well: it applies only to a person 18 years of age or over, only where more than half the working time is spent away from the employer’s place of business, and only where the away-from-the-premises work is selling items or obtaining orders or contracts. Other California overtime exemptions — the executive, administrative, and professional exemptions, the commissioned inside sales exemption, and the computer software employee exemption — have their own separate requirements and are addressed by other documents in this corpus.

expectedJSON.body: Acme, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe what California law says about the outside salesperson exemption from the state’s wage and hour requirements — the exemption that is in question for a position such as Territory Sales Representative, held by Jordan Lee. It describes the statutory exclusion in Labor Code section 1171; the Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders’ definition of “outside salesperson” and the provision stating that the orders do not apply to such employees; the absence of any salary condition in that provision; the California Supreme Court’s holding in Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. that California uses a quantitative more-than-half-the-working-time test rather than the federal “primary function” test; how working time is counted, including travel time and delivery work; the “realistic requirements of the job” rule; the narrow construction of overtime exemptions and the employer’s burden of proof; and the limits of what the exclusion reaches. It describes the law; it does not classify any employee as exempt or nonexempt and does not evaluate any particular job.

California’s wage, hour, and working-conditions statutes for employees are gathered in Chapter 1 of Part 4 of Division 2 of the Labor Code, sections 1171 through 1207. The first section of that chapter, section 1171, states the chapter’s coverage: it applies to men, women, and minors employed in any occupation, trade, or industry, whether compensation is measured by time, piece, or otherwise, but it does not include any individual employed as an outside salesman, or any individual participating in a national service program carried out with assistance under section 12571 of title 42 of the United States Code.

Section 1171 does not itself define “outside salesman.” The definition used in California comes from the Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders, which are described in the next clause. In Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co., the California Supreme Court framed the question before it as whether an employee who performs a mixture of sales and nonsales duties is an “outside salesperson” within the meaning of section 1171, and described the answer as turning on a detailed, fact-specific determination of how the employee spent his time.

expectedJSON.body:
In Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co., the California Supreme Court held that the state’s outside salesperson definition is not to be read through the federal regulations. The federal exemption in effect at that time asked what the employee’s chief duty or primary function was, and then treated all work incidental to and in conjunction with the employee’s own sales — including incidental deliveries and collections — as exempt work. The court described the federal test as focused on defining the employee’s “primary function,” not on how much work time is spent selling.

The California wage order, the court explained, contains no provision that reclassifies intrinsically nonexempt nonsales work as exempt on the ground that it is incidental to sales. The court concluded that by adopting a distinct definition rather than tracking the federal language, the Industrial Welfare Commission intended to depart from federal law and to provide, at least in some cases, greater protection for employees. A court or a trier of fact applying the California definition therefore measures the share of working time spent on the activities the definition names, rather than characterizing the job as a whole.

citations.case: Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785 (CourtListener text)
citations.quote: Thus, the federal exemption focuses on defining the employee’s “primary function,” not on how much work time is spent selling.

citations.case: Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785 (CourtListener text)
citations.quote: State law also differs from the federal regulation in that it does not contain any provision that reclassifies intrinsically nonexempt nonsales work as exempt based on the fact that it is incidental to sales.

citations.case: Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785 (CourtListener text)
citations.quote: By choosing not to track the language of the federal exemption and instead adopting its own distinct definition of “outside salespersons,” the IWC evidently intended to depart from federal law and to provide, at least in some cases, greater protection for employees.

expectedJSON.body:
Because the California test is quantitative, Ramirez addressed how the hours are to be counted: by the employer’s job description and estimate of what the employee should be doing, or by the hours the employee actually spent. The court held that neither alternative alone is satisfactory. Counting by the job description would let an employer make an employee exempt simply by writing an idealized description with little basis in reality; counting only actual hours would let an employee who falls below the 50 percent mark through his or her own substandard performance escape an otherwise valid exemption.

The court resolved the problem by directing the trier of fact to inquire into the realistic requirements of the job: to consider, first and foremost, how the employee actually spends his or her time, and also whether the employee’s practice diverges from the employer’s realistic expectations, whether there was any concrete expression of employer displeasure over substandard performance, and whether those expressions were themselves realistic given the actual overall requirements of the job.

citations.case: Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785 (CourtListener text)
citations.quote: On the one hand, if hours worked on sales were determined through an employer’s job description, then the employer could make an employee exempt from overtime laws solely by fashioning an idealized job description that had little basis in reality. On the other hand, an employee who is supposed to be engaged in sales activities during most of his working hours and falls below the 50 percent mark due to his own substandard performance should not thereby be able to evade a valid exemption.

citations.case: Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785 (CourtListener text)
citations.quote: A trial court, in determining whether the employee is an outside salesperson, must steer clear of these two pitfalls by inquiring into the realistic requirements of the job. In so doing, the court should consider, first and foremost, how the employee actually spends his or her time. But the trial court should also consider whether the employee’s practice diverges from the employer’s realistic expectations, whether there was any concrete expression of employer displeasure over an employee’s substandard performance, and whether these expressions were themselves realistic given the actual overall requirements of the job.

The same “realistic requirements of the job” language was later written into section 1(A) of the wage orders for the executive, administrative, and professional exemptions, which are separate exemptions addressed by other documents in this corpus and not by this one. How any particular employee’s time was in fact spent is a question of fact that this document does not address.

expectedJSON.body:
The employer in Ramirez argued that a strict reading of the wage order would produce an absurd result, because even full-time salespeople spend much of the day on preparation, travel, and paperwork rather than on face-to-face selling. The California Supreme Court answered that the order need not be read that strictly. Travel undertaken in order to attempt a sale counts as time spent selling: the court gave the example of a salesperson who must travel one hour to a destination to attempt a sale, and said the most reasonable interpretation of the wage order is to count that hour of travel as time spent selling.

Where a single trip serves both purposes, the court held that the travel time must be apportioned between the two types of activity for purposes of determining the total amount of time spent doing sales and nonsales work.

citations.case: Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785 (CourtListener text)
citations.quote: If a salesperson must travel one hour to destination A in order to attempt a sale, then surely the most reasonable interpretation of the wage order is to count the hour of travel time as time spent “selling.” But if, as in the present case, an employee travels to a destination to engage in both sales and nonsales activities, the travel time must be apportioned among the two types of activities for purposes of determining the total amount of time spent doing sales and nonsales work.

expectedJSON.gap: The court did not state a formula or method for apportioning travel time on a mixed trip, and no source cited in this document supplies one. Whether travel time is compensable hours worked for an employee who is not an outside salesperson is a different question governed by other authority (including Morillion v. Royal Packing Co. and the wage orders’ “hours worked” definition) that this clause does not address; the passage quoted here goes only to whether travel counts toward the more-than-half measure in the outside salesperson definition. The characterization of the employer’s argument in the body summarizes the opinion’s description of that argument.

expectedJSON.body:
Ramirez involved a route sales representative who delivered bottled water and was also expected to sign up new customers. The California Supreme Court stated that delivering preordered water bottles or restocking empties is not a sales activity in the conventional meaning of the word, and that a person who only performed those delivery tasks could not be considered a salesperson. The court rejected the argument that delivery becomes a sales activity because poor delivery would cost the customer, comparing that reasoning to treating an attorney’s preparation of a brief as a sales activity because it keeps the client.

Because the trial court and the Court of Appeal had applied the federal standard, or a hybrid of the federal and state standards, the Supreme Court reversed and remanded rather than deciding the employee’s status itself.

citations.case: Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 785 (CourtListener text)
citations.quote: Delivery of preordered water bottles or the restocking of “empties” is not a sales activity in the conventional meaning of the word—one who only performed these delivery tasks could not be considered a salesperson. It is true, as Yosemite points out, that failure to properly deliver the product would lead to loss of the customer, but that does not make such delivery a sales activity, any more than an attorney’s preparation of a legal brief in order to satisfy and thereby retain a client is a sales activity.

expectedJSON.body: Ramirez set out two general principles before construing the exemption. First, because the statutes regulating wages, hours, and working conditions are remedial and are liberally construed to promote the protection of employees, exemptions from the state’s mandatory overtime provisions are narrowly construed. Second, the assertion of an exemption from the overtime laws is an affirmative defense, so the employer bears the burden of proving the employee’s exemption.

expectedJSON.body:
The employer in Ramirez argued that the Industrial Welfare Commission had exceeded its authority by adopting a definition of “outside salesperson” narrower than the federal one, since the Legislature had borrowed a term already defined in federal law. The California Supreme Court rejected the argument. It held that the definition was within the scope of the Commission’s authority and was reasonably necessary to effectuate the purpose of section 1171: some working definition was needed because employees often work in both sales and nonsales capacities, and it was reasonable for the Commission to take a quantitative approach, looking to the actual hours spent on sales activity. The court added that the definition would be entitled to deference in any event, having been adopted through public notice and comment and consistently maintained for nearly 20 years.

The Legislature has separately referred to the outside salesperson category in Labor Code section 517, subdivision (d), which directed the Commission to conduct a review of the wages, hours, and working conditions of outside salespersons notwithstanding section 1171 and section 515, subdivision (a).

citations.quote: It was necessary for the IWC to establish some working definition of “outside salesperson” that takes into account the fact that some employees work in both sales and nonsales capacities. It was reasonable for the IWC, in formulating its definition, to take a quantitative approach, looking to the actual hours spent on sales activity to determine if an employee is primarily a salesperson.

The exclusion described in this document is bounded in several ways that appear on the face of the authorities. Labor Code section 1171 excludes an outside salesman from “this chapter” only — Chapter 1 of Part 4 of Division 2 of the Labor Code. It says nothing about Labor Code provisions located in other chapters, parts, or divisions, and nothing about federal law, local ordinances, or contract terms. Wage order section 1(C) makes the provisions of that order inapplicable, and each order covers only the industries or occupations its Section 1 describes.

The definition itself sets limits as well: it applies only to a person 18 years of age or over, only where more than half the working time is spent away from the employer’s place of business, and only where the away-from-the-premises work is selling items or obtaining orders or contracts. Other California overtime exemptions — the executive, administrative, and professional exemptions, the commissioned inside sales exemption, and the computer software employee exemption — have their own separate requirements and are addressed by other documents in this corpus.
